title: A self-hosted colleague in a Teams call
subtitle: Bridging Microsoft's real-time media stack to a voice AI that never leaves my own hardware

stats.label: buffers per second across the soak, against 20 ms pacing
the single retry in a forced mid-call reconnect
round-trip media latency at most in a single probe, 65 at least

lede: I rang a Microsoft Teams number, a digital employee answered, and we had a two-way spoken conversation. The speech recognition, the conversation engine and the voice all ran on GPUs in my own rack. Nothing about the call touched a third-party AI cloud. Making that possible meant building a bridge between two worlds that were never designed to meet: Microsoft's Windows-only real-time media stack and a Linux voice engine, joined by a purpose-built audio link that survived a thirty-minute soak and a forced mid-call reconnect before I would call it done. Microsoft Teams will hand raw call audio to a bot, and only to a Windows application built on Microsoft's real-time media SDK.
quote: Replaying produces a colleague who answers a question from twenty seconds ago.
evidence: Microsoft Teams real-time media: a self-hosted AI colleague in Teams calls through a Windows media bridge on Azure, carrying 20 ms buffers at 50.001 per second with no receive stalls.
Binary wire protocol design: one authenticated full-duplex audio link per call, implemented in C# and in Rust and proven byte-identical against golden test vectors.
Distributed systems correctness: a forced mid-call reconnect resumed the same call after a single 250 ms retry, dropping audio from the gap instead of replaying it.
Real-time voice AI on local GPUs: recognition, conversation and voice kept on my own hardware behind the engine's existing audio seam, with 65 to 67 ms round-trip media latency.
author: Corey James
